measures.summary: Approves a county property tax rate of $0.24865 per $100 of value, 2.4 cents above the rate the county can set without voter approval. The ballot calls it a tax increase.

paxton.name: Ken Paxton
paxton.summary: Attorney general since 2015 after 10 years in the Texas House and two in the Texas Senate. Won the May 26 Republican runoff over Sen. John Cornyn with 63.8% after President Trump endorsed him. He was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted on all charges by the Texas Senate. Did not answer the Texas Tribune questionnaire, so positions below come from his past public statements.

positions.stance: Supports permanently repealing the federal gas tax and keeping oil and gas regulation low to raise production.
Supports efficient water use, having the industry pay its own infrastructure costs, ending state sales tax breaks, and keeping facilities away from homes.
Backs the president's actions on Iran; says he will decide on funding after getting more intelligence.
Called the plans "not smart border security" and welcomed the August pause.
Opposes it; as attorney general he extended the state ban to mental health providers.
Has sued Dallas over marijuana decriminalization; no direct comment found on Texas THC rules.

Supports legal, regulated adult marijuana with taxes funding public safety and health programs.

h20-edgardo-rafael-baez.name: Edgardo Rafael Baez
h20-edgardo-rafael-baez.occupation: Attorney; U.S. Army veteran and former intensive care unit nurse
h20-edgardo-rafael-baez.summary: Edgardo Rafael Báez is a San Antonio attorney who was born in Ponce, Puerto Rico. He served in the U.S. Army as a combat medic, paratrooper and drill sergeant, and later worked as an intensive care unit nurse. In his first run for office, he won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary for Texas' 20th Congressional District without an opponent, and he will face Democratic incumbent Joaquin Castro on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot.

positions.stance: Wants to bring the federal deficit down to 3% of GDP or less by 2030 through spending cuts and revenue measures. Opposes broad stimulus such as $2,000 tariff rebate checks, which he compares to COVID-era stimulus that he says drove inflation.

Supports reforming Social Security and Medicare to deal with projected trust fund shortfalls. Lists options such as raising retirement ages, means-testing benefits, or slowing entitlement growth without raising taxes.

Wants Congress to put border security, interior enforcement and the protection of American workers first. Opposes amnesty and any path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. Also proposes a merit-based legal immigration system tied to workforce needs.
Opposes closing the Dilley Immigration Processing Center. He argues that cutting detention capacity without stronger border security would not solve the problem.
Wants to change the Affordable Care Act without large subsidies, which he says mainly benefit big insurance companies. Supports an open market where people can choose from many health plans.
Names public safety as a top priority, citing violent and property crime rates, homelessness and repeat offending among young people in the district.
Calls for better reading and math programs and points to F-rated schools in the district. Says schools are teaching 'doctrines' instead of core subjects like English, math and science.

Says he has written 11 bills to introduce if elected, including veterans-related legislation. Said he was undecided on the Major Richard Star Act and the Take Care of America's Veterans Act until he could review where the funding goes.

Would support or introduce War Powers Resolutions requiring Congress to approve further military action. Would use appropriations to withhold money for unauthorized operations, and would back bipartisan legislation barring funds to occupy or annex Greenland.

Attorney practicing family and criminal law in San Antonio for about 20 years; now runs a law firm with his wife

Former pastor at a San Antonio church
No previous elected office

h20-joaquin-castro.name: Joaquin Castro
h20-joaquin-castro.occupation: U.S. Representative for Texas' 20th Congressional District; attorney and former law professor
h20-joaquin-castro.summary: Joaquin Castro is a Democrat from San Antonio. He has represented Texas' 20th Congressional District since 2013, and before that he served in the Texas House of Representatives from 2003 to 2013. He won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary with 88.2% of the vote against Kendra Wilkerson and John Atwood, and he faces Republican Edgardo Baez in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Opposes the family detention center in Dilley, Texas, which he calls the 'Dilley Trailer Prison.' He says children held there have suffered lasting trauma, and in October 2026 he invited President Trump to visit the facility during a trip to San Antonio.
Joined other members of the San Antonio congressional delegation in urging cities to end their 287(g) agreements with ICE. (Based on the press release title only.)

Voted against the Laken Riley Act (S.5, 2025). The law requires DHS to detain certain undocumented immigrants arrested for theft-related offenses and lets states sue the federal government over immigration enforcement.

Voted against H.R. 1, the 2025 reconciliation law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Also voted against the FY2025 budget resolution (H.Con.Res.14), which set up that reconciliation process and the debt-limit increase.

Voted against the full-year continuing appropriations act for FY2025 (H.R.1968). Also voted against the November 2025 continuing resolution (H.R.5371) that ended the government shutdown that began October 1, 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22, 2025), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
Voted against the No Rogue Rulings Act (H.R.1526, 2025), which would limit federal district court injunctions to the parties in a case.

h21-mark-teixeira.occupation: Former Major League Baseball player; investor in small businesses, startups and real estate
h21-mark-teixeira.summary: Mark Teixeira is a former Major League Baseball first baseman who played for the Texas Rangers, Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Angels and New York Yankees, and later worked as an ESPN analyst and investor. He won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary for Texas' 21st Congressional District outright with 60.9% of the vote against 11 other candidates, for the open seat held by U.S. Rep. Chip Roy. He faces Democrat Kristin Hook in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Supports stronger border enforcement and deportations.

Proposes expanding DOGE to cut what he calls wasteful federal spending, and calls for more auditing and oversight of public spending. Wants to reduce the deficit through spending cuts rather than raising tax rates.
Opposes raising tax rates to address the deficit and supports spending cuts instead, according to the Austin American-Statesman editorial board's account of his position.
Proposes expanding Texas oil, gas and nuclear production to restore U.S. 'energy dominance' and lower costs for families. Supports federal support for grid modernization, research and infrastructure.

Says he wants to lower health care costs, expand consumer choice and reduce Washington's control over health care decisions. Proposes targeting fraud, waste and abuse in Medicare and Medicaid, limiting program care to eligible citizens, and opening insurance markets to more competition.

Says elective abortion should be allowed only when the mother's life is threatened. Opposes taxpayer funding for abortion providers, including Planned Parenthood, and supports enforcing the Comstock Act's ban on shipping abortion-inducing drugs across state lines.
Supports school choice and empowering parents in education. Supports eliminating the U.S. Department of Education and returning control to states and communities.
His platform supports gun rights.
Supports congressional term limits.
Says marriage is a union of one man and one woman. Agrees with the statement that physically or socially transitioning a child to the opposite sex is child abuse.

h21-kristin-hook.name: Kristin Hook
h21-kristin-hook.occupation: Scientist (former U.S. Government Accountability Office biologist)
h21-kristin-hook.summary: Kristin Hook is a biologist from Corpus Christi with a Ph.D. from Cornell. She worked in federal science and oversight jobs, including at the U.S. Government Accountability Office and as an oversight investigator for Sen. Elizabeth Warren. She was the Democratic nominee for Texas' 21st Congressional District in 2024, won the three-way Democratic primary on March 3, 2026, and faces Republican Mark Teixeira for the open seat on November 3, 2026.

positions.stance: Supports changing the tax code so that, in her words, 'the wealthy pay their fair share.' Her campaign's economic platform is titled 'Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share.'
Supports passing federal legislation to restore abortion rights nationwide and to protect access to contraception and IVF. Her campaign platform is titled 'Abortion: Restoring Our Freedoms.'
Pledges to strengthen public schools and workforce training programs. Supports partnerships between employers and schools to train workers.
Says she will 'stop AI data centers from stealing our water and electricity.' Pledges to protect the environment and clean water.
Supports raising the federal minimum wage and lowering the cost of housing, health care, child care, elder care and groceries. Supports strengthening Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security.

positions.topic: Congressional oversight and separation of powers
positions.stance: Says Congress should check the executive branch rather than defer to it. Supports oversight investigations, open hearings and use of the power of the purse.

h23-brandon-herrera.name: Brandon Herrera
h23-brandon-herrera.occupation: Firearms manufacturer and YouTube content creator
h23-brandon-herrera.summary: Brandon Herrera is a firearms manufacturer and YouTube personality known online as "The AK Guy." He advanced to a runoff with incumbent Rep. Tony Gonzales in the March 3, 2026 Republican primary for Texas' 23rd Congressional District. Gonzales later ended his re-election campaign and resigned, and Herrera is the Republican nominee on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot against Katy Padilla Stout (D) and Ben Mendoza (I).

positions.stance: Pledges to oppose any spending bill that does not fund completion of the border wall, and supports reinstating the "Remain in Mexico" policy and ending what he calls abuse of the asylum system.
Opposes border wall construction in the Big Bend region. His campaign calls a physical wall there unnecessary because of the area's rugged terrain, and he welcomed a pause on construction there.
Pledges no new taxes, says he will cut wasteful spending, and supports the REINS Act.
Supports national concealed carry reciprocity and says he wants to expand gun rights.
When asked about the Uvalde shooting in a debate, he asked why the state did not have armed security at schools to protect children.
Said in a debate that West Texas has become "ground zero" for data centers in the country.
Proposes better access to services and support for veterans and their families.

h23-katy-padilla-stout.name: Katy Padilla Stout
h23-katy-padilla-stout.occupation: Attorney who represents children in foster care; former public school teacher
h23-katy-padilla-stout.summary: Katy Padilla Stout is a San Antonio attorney who represents children in the foster care system and has served on the Bexar County Child Welfare Board since 2017. Before law school she taught elementary school in Northside ISD. She won a four-way Democratic primary in March 2026 and is the Democratic nominee for Texas' 23rd Congressional District, the seat left open after Rep. Tony Gonzales left office; this is her first run for office.

positions.stance: Says the region needs "a functioning border," neither closed nor open, with security that keeps lawful commerce and cooperation with Mexico. Supports pathways to citizenship and border security that does not rely mainly on detention, deportation and physical barriers.

Opposes tax cuts for billionaires and supports a tax code she says would strengthen the middle class. Supports legislation limiting the President's power to impose tariffs on his own, and supports universal Pre-K and paid parental leave funded through existing unemployment insurance programs.
Supports raising the minimum age to buy what she called "assault weapons" to 21 (stated in the October 13 debate).
Supports more funding for mental health services. In the debate she argued that adding armed security is not enough, pointing to the police response at the Uvalde shooting.

Calls for a pause on building new data centers until Congress passes laws protecting water supplies, the electric grid and taxpayers. Questions large tax incentives given to developers in exchange for few permanent jobs.

Supports expanding Medicare to cover all Americans and, short of that, strengthening the Affordable Care Act. Supports expanding federal community health centers, investing in rural hospitals, and student loan forgiveness for doctors and nurses who work in rural facilities.
